VIDEO.title: The Hidden Battle Between Jesus and Satan That Most MISS! (Matthew 4:1-11)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: Bread, a leap, a kingdom, and three times: “It is written.”
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 4:1-11: the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, He fasts forty days and nights, and the tempter tests Him three times. Each time Jesus answers, 'It is written,' quoting Deuteronomy. Then the devil leaves and angels minister to Him.

Three tests, three expressions of one idea: what it means to be the Son of God. Food (appetite), rescue at the temple (affirmation from the Father), and the kingdoms of the world (power and ambition).

The temptation is the culmination of a thread Matthew has woven since chapter 1: Jesus linked to Abraham, a Pharaoh-like Herod, a child hidden in Egypt, a baptism 'to fulfill all righteousness,' and the Father's voice, 'This is My beloved Son,' just as God called Israel His son.

Like Israel, Jesus is led into the wilderness (the cloud and fire, Exodus 13:21), is hungry, and is tested. His answer about testing God points back to Massah, where Israel asked, 'Is Yahweh among us or not?' (Exodus 17:7).

Behind it all is desire: Israel 'asking for food according to their desire' (Psalm 78:18) and Eve seeing that the tree was 'good for food' (Genesis 3:6). Where Adam, Eve and Israel gave in, Jesus, standing in Israel's place, says no.

The lesson for the first hearers and for us: God's people need to be so filled and satisfied with the word of God that they stand firm in trusting Him, even in temptation. Like the Creator who rested, we learn to know when enough is enough.
QUOTES: The first time Jesus is tempted with food, the second time Jesus is tempted with rescue, and the third time with power.
Jesus' temptation in the wilderness is the culmination of a thematic thread that Matthew has been weaving from the very start of his gospel.

Eve succumbed to her desires. Israel succumbed to their desires... Jesus, standing in the place of Israel as the suffering, chosen servant of Yahweh, goes through the same experiences, but this time He denies those desires.
God's people need to be so filled and satisfied with the word of God that they can stand firm in trusting Him, even in the midst of temptation.
This is the kind of God who knows when enough is enough... knowing how to say to our passions: no, I will not be ruled by you.

method.h: Read it as the first hearers did
method.p: Matthew's first hearers knew the Exodus story and the garden of Genesis 3 by heart, and they probably heard this Gospel read aloud in church. So the teacher asks one question of verses 1-11: by telling this story, what is Matthew teaching the reader about Jesus? Listen for Israel's wilderness and Eden's garden behind every line.
method.mark: what is Matthew teaching the reader about Jesus?

LSB_QUOTES.text: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
It is written, ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God.’
Go, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve Him only.’
Then the devil left Him; and behold, angels came and began to minister to Him.

TESTS.title: Stones into bread
TESTS.offer: If You are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread.
TESTS.answer: It is written, ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God.’
TESTS.srcText: And He humbled you and let you be hungry and fed you with manna which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that He might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by everything that proceeds out of the mouth of Yahweh.
TESTS.israel: Yahweh let Israel be hungry and fed them manna, 'testing you, to know what was in your heart' (Deuteronomy 8:2-3). Later they 'put God to the test by asking for food according to their desire' (Psalm 78:18).
TESTS.note: The video: Satan tempts Jesus to use His 'son-of-God-ness' to eat. Jesus is truly hungry (4:2) and still trusts His Father to feed Him.

TESTS.title: A leap from the temple
TESTS.offer: If You are the Son of God, throw Yourself down; for it is written, / ‘He will command His angels concerning You’; and / ‘On their hands they will bear You up, / Lest You strike Your foot against a stone.’
TESTS.answer: Again, it is written, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’
TESTS.srcText: You shall not put Yahweh your God to the test, as you tested Him at Massah.
TESTS.misused: The devil quotes Psalm 91:11-12. The next line reads: 'You will tread upon the fierce lion and cobra, / The young lion and the serpent you will trample down' (91:13).
TESTS.israel: At Massah Israel 'tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us or not?”' (Exodus 17:7). The video: with the Father not visibly present, Satan invites Jesus to force Him to show up.
TESTS.note: Jesus will not stage a test to prove the Father is with Him. Later He says He could appeal to His Father for 'more than twelve legions of angels' (Matthew 26:53), and still chooses the cross.

TESTS.title: All the kingdoms of the world
TESTS.offer: All these things I will give You, if You fall down and worship me.
TESTS.answer: Go, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve Him only.’
TESTS.srcText: Yahweh your God you shall fear; and Him you shall serve; and by His name you shall swear.
TESTS.israel: The next verse warns, 'You shall not walk after other gods' (Deuteronomy 6:14). At Sinai Israel 'made for themselves a molten calf and have worshiped it' (Exodus 32:8).
TESTS.note: Matthew's wording ('worship... Him only') follows the Greek Old Testament tradition rather than the Hebrew 'fear.' The kingdoms Satan offers, Jesus receives later from the Father by way of the cross: 'All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth' (28:18).

EDEN.h: Back to the garden: the same desires
EDEN.text: Then the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was desirable to make one wise, so she took from its fruit and ate; and she gave also to her husband with her, and he ate.
EDEN.video: The teacher reads Genesis 3:6 and tracks the language of desire. Eve gave in, Israel gave in, all of us have given in; Jesus, the faithful Son, did not.
EDEN.added: Some readers also line up the three tests with 'the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes and the boastful pride of life' (1 John 2:16) or with the three phrases of Genesis 3:6. The parallel is suggestive; a one-to-one match is debated. Paul draws the larger contrast: 'through the one man’s disobedience the many were appointed sinners, even so through the obedience of the One the many will be appointed righteous' (Romans 5:19).

ECHOES.now: The Father: 'This is My beloved Son' (3:17). The tempter: 'If You are the Son of God' (4:3, 6).

ECHOES.now: 'Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness.'

ECHOES.now: 'After He had fasted forty days and forty nights, He then became hungry.'

ECHOES.then: 'He humbled you and let you be hungry and fed you with manna.'
ECHOES.now: Hungry, Jesus refuses to make bread for Himself and quotes this very verse.

ECHOES.then: Israel 'tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us or not?”'

PEOPLE.name: Jesus
PEOPLE.video: The beloved Son standing in the place of Israel, Yahweh's chosen servant. Where Adam, Eve and Israel gave in to desire, He refuses, answering each test with Scripture.
PEOPLE.bg: 'One who has been tempted in all things like we are, yet without sin' (Hebrews 4:15). 'He is able to come to help those who are tempted' (Hebrews 2:18).

PEOPLE.name: The devil, the tempter, Satan
PEOPLE.video: He strikes three times at one idea: what it means to be the Son of God.
PEOPLE.bg: Matthew uses three names: 'the devil' (4:1, Greek diabolos), 'the tempter' (4:3) and 'Satan' (4:10, from Hebrew satan, 'adversary'). In the Old Testament the satan appears as an accuser in Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3. Luke adds that he left Jesus 'until an opportune time' (Luke 4:13).

PEOPLE.name: The Spirit
PEOPLE.video: Leads Jesus into the wilderness, as the cloud and fire led Israel.
PEOPLE.bg: Mark is stronger: 'the Spirit drove Him to go out into the wilderness' (Mark 1:12). Luke: Jesus was 'full of the Holy Spirit' (Luke 4:1). The same Spirit came down on Him at His baptism (3:16).

PEOPLE.name: Angels
PEOPLE.video: After the devil leaves, 'angels came and began to minister to Him' (4:11).
PEOPLE.bg: The verb (diakoneō) is also used for waiting on someone at a meal (8:15). Jesus would not force Psalm 91's angels to catch Him; afterward His Father sends them. Mark adds that 'He was with the wild beasts' (Mark 1:13).

PEOPLE.name: Israel in the wilderness
PEOPLE.video: God's son, led by the cloud, tested by hunger, and failing by desire (Exodus 13, 17; Psalm 78).
PEOPLE.bg: Deuteronomy 8:5: 'Yahweh your God was disciplining you just as a man disciplines his son.' All three of Jesus' answers come from Moses' sermons to this generation (Deuteronomy 6-8).

PEOPLE.name: Adam and Eve
PEOPLE.video: The first humans, enticed by the serpent and led by desire (Genesis 3:6).
PEOPLE.bg: Irenaeus (2nd century) reads the temptation as Jesus 're-running' Adam's test and winning it (see Early witnesses). Paul contrasts 'the one man's disobedience' with 'the obedience of the One' (Romans 5:19).

PEOPLE.name: Moses and Elijah
PEOPLE.video: The video compares the child Jesus, hidden from a murderous tyrant, to Moses. It does not mention their forty-day fasts.
PEOPLE.bg: Moses was on the mountain 'forty days and forty nights; he did not eat bread or drink water' (Exodus 34:28). Elijah went 'forty days and forty nights to Horeb' (1 Kings 19:8). Both later appear with Jesus on the mountain (17:3).

TERMS.def: One Greek verb (peirazō) covers both. God tests to prove and strengthen (Deuteronomy 8:2); the devil tempts to make someone fall. 'God cannot be tempted by evil, and He Himself does not tempt anyone' (James 1:13).

TERMS.term: If You are the Son of God
TERMS.def: The question behind all three tests. The Father has just said 'This is My beloved Son' (3:17); the tempter does not deny it but pushes Jesus to use His sonship for Himself. The same taunt returns at the cross: 'If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross' (27:40).
Jesus' answer three times. The Greek perfect tense means 'it stands written': settled and still in force. All three quotations come from Deuteronomy 6-8.

The video promises to return to numbers but does not. Forty marks testing and preparation: the flood (Genesis 7:12), Moses on the mountain (Exodus 34:28), Israel's forty years (Deuteronomy 8:2), Elijah (1 Kings 19:8).
Jerusalem. Matthew uses the phrase again in 27:53.
Literally 'little wing' (pterygion), some high edge of the temple complex. Matthew does not say which; many think of the southeast corner above the Kidron Valley.
Matthew names no mountain; no single peak shows 'all the kingdoms of the world.' Mountains matter in Matthew: the sermon (5:1), the transfiguration (17:1), the commission (28:16).
'Testing,' the place where Israel quarreled and asked, 'Is Yahweh among us or not?' (Exodus 17:7). Deuteronomy 6:16, which Jesus quotes, names it.

The video's key word. Eve saw the tree was 'desirable' (Genesis 3:6); Israel asked for food 'according to their desire' (Psalm 78:18). 'Each one is tempted when he is carried away and enticed by his own lust' (James 1:14).

WORDS.gloss: To test, try; to tempt. The same verb gives 'to be tempted' (4:1) and 'the tempter' (4:3, ho peirazōn, 'the one testing'). Context decides between testing and tempting. Look up: BDAG, πειράζω.
To put to the test. A strengthened form of peirazō, used in the Greek Old Testament of Deuteronomy 6:16 and quoted here. Look up: BDAG, ἐκπειράζω.
As an adjective 'slanderous'; as a noun 'slanderer,' and in the New Testament 'the devil.' Look up: BDAG, διάβολος.
Satan, the Greek form of Hebrew satan, 'adversary.' Jesus' 'Go' (hypage) here is the same word as 'Get behind Me, Satan!' to Peter (16:23).
Diminutive of pteryx, 'wing': a tip or edge, here a high point of the temple. Which spot is meant is uncertain. Look up: BDAG, πτερύγιον.
To bow down, prostrate oneself; to worship. The magi came to 'worship' Jesus (2:2, 11); Satan asks Jesus to 'fall down and worship' him.
To serve, especially in worship. Translates Hebrew 'abad' (serve) in Deuteronomy 6:13.
To serve, wait on, minister; used of serving at a meal. The angels 'began to minister' after His long hunger (4:11; compare 8:15).
Word, saying, something spoken. 'Every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God' (4:4), the verse behind the channel's name.
To test, try, prove. Used for God testing Israel (Deuteronomy 8:2) and Israel testing God (Exodus 17:7; Deuteronomy 6:16). Look up: BDB or HALOT, נסה.
'Testing,' a place name from nasah. Exodus 17:7 explains the name: 'because they tested Yahweh.'
That which goes out, an utterance. 'Everything that proceeds out of the mouth of Yahweh' (Deuteronomy 8:3). Look up: BDB or HALOT, מוֹצָא.
To work, serve; also to serve in worship. 'Him you shall serve' (Deuteronomy 6:13).
Adversary, accuser; with the article, 'the satan' (Job 1:6; Zechariah 3:1). Look up: BDB or HALOT, שָׂטָן.

BACKGROUND.p: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell preaching to Israel on the plains of Moab, after forty years in the wilderness. Jesus quotes 8:3, 6:16 and 6:13, close to the Shema: 'Hear, O Israel! Yahweh is our God, Yahweh is one! You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart' (6:4-5). Matthew's wording follows the Greek Old Testament: 'every word' (8:3) and 'worship... Him only' (6:13).

Mark gives two verses (1:12-13). Matthew and Luke give the three tests, but Luke has the temple last (Luke 4:5-12), while Matthew ends on the mountain, with worship. Matthew links the scene to the baptism: 'Then' (4:1).

BACKGROUND.h: The temple Satan stood Him on
BACKGROUND.p: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple and its courts in his eighteenth year, about 20/19 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 15.11.1). Josephus describes the royal portico on the south side as so high above the valley that anyone looking down would grow dizzy (Antiquities 15.11.5).

Moses (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 9:9) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:8) both went forty days without ordinary food. Matthew says Jesus 'fasted' (4:2); Luke says 'He ate nothing during those days' (Luke 4:2). Only afterward did He become hungry.
A psalm of trust: whoever shelters in the Most High is guarded by His angels. The devil quotes 91:11-12 as a dare. The psalm's promise is for those who trust God, not for those who test Him.

WITNESSES.text: For as at the beginning it was by means of food that [the enemy] persuaded man, although not suffering hunger, to transgress God's commandments, so in the end he did not succeed in persuading Him that was an hungered to take that food which proceeded from God.
WITNESSES.src: Against Heresies 5.21.2, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (public domain). Of the second test he writes that the devil was 'concealing a falsehood under the guise of Scripture.'

WITNESSES.text: Then. When? After the descent of the Spirit, after the voice that was borne from above, and said, This is My Beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 13, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain). He also says Jesus answered 'bringing him a testimony out of the ancient Scripture.'

DEBATES.p: Luke has the temple last; Matthew has the mountain last. Many think Matthew's order builds to the climax of worship ('Go, Satan!'), while Luke's ends at Jerusalem, the goal of his Gospel. Neither writer says his order is chronological.

No mountain shows 'all the kingdoms of the world,' so some read the second and third tests as visionary. Others take the journeys as real, with the 'showing' supernatural. Matthew says the devil 'took Him' (4:5, 8) and does not explain how.

Hebrews says He was tempted 'in all things like we are, yet without sin' (4:15). Theologians differ on whether He was able not to sin or not able to sin; all agree the testing was real. The video puts it simply: 'Jesus is the God-man, and there are things only He could go through.'

DEBATES.h: Do the three tests match Genesis 3:6 or 1 John 2:16?
DEBATES.p: Some line up food, eyes and pride one for one; others think that is too neat. The video links them more loosely, through the language of desire.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says Herod 'killed firstborns.' Matthew 2:16 says he killed 'all the male children who were in Bethlehem and all its vicinity, from two years old and under.' Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew son killed (Exodus 1:22); the death of the firstborn was the tenth plague, on Egypt (Exodus 12:29). The Pharaoh parallel still holds.
The video promises, 'We're going to get into numbers and what they mean later,' but does not come back to the forty days. See Key terms and the Timeline for a start.
The video calls Matthew 'probably a letter that's being read to the church.' Matthew is a Gospel, not a letter, though the teacher's point stands: it was likely heard read aloud by early believers.
Among the Isaiah references, the video lists 'the true vine' (John 15:1). The words are Jesus' own in John; the Old Testament picture behind them is Israel as God's vine (Psalm 80:8; Isaiah 5:1-7).
The captions read 'Matthew 4:1-1'; the passage is Matthew 4:1-11.

TIMELINE.what: The serpent tempts Eve; desire leads to the first sin
Rain for forty days and forty nights
Israel, God's son, leaves Egypt led by cloud and fire; tests Yahweh at Massah
Moses on the mountain forty days and nights without bread; the golden calf below
Moses preaches Deuteronomy on the plains of Moab; views the land from Mount Nebo
Elijah goes forty days and nights to Horeb
Herod the Great begins rebuilding the temple
Jesus is baptized, then tested forty days in the wilderness
After His resurrection, Jesus appears to the apostles over forty days

QUESTIONS: The video's own challenge: 'If God's people need to be so filled and satisfied with the word of God that they can stand firm in trusting Him even in the midst of temptation, then will you?' What would that look like for you this week?
All three of Jesus' answers come from Deuteronomy 6-8. Read those three chapters. What else there would have strengthened Him, and you?
Appetite, affirmation, ambition: which of the three hits closest to home? Where do you need to tell a desire, 'No, I will not be ruled by you'?
The devil quoted Scripture too (Psalm 91). How can you tell Scripture used rightly from Scripture twisted? Read Psalm 91 whole and compare.
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The video's lesson for the original audience: to withstand the devil, who entices God's people to give in to their own desires, we must be filled with the word of God and so satisfied with it that we stand firm in trusting the Lord, His provision and His plans. Where mankind failed, Jesus succeeded. Like our Creator, who stopped and saw that His work was good, we learn to know when enough is enough. The lesson for you: will you be filled and satisfied with the word of God?
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): Jesus did not invent new weapons; He used verses Israel had known for centuries, in context. Treasure the word now, before the test comes: 'Your word I have treasured in my heart, / That I may not sin against You' (Psalm 119:11). 'The sword of the Spirit... is the word of God' (Ephesians 6:17). And when you fail, the One who passed the test is 'able to come to help those who are tempted' (Hebrews 2:18; see 1 Corinthians 10:13).

PLACES.name: Jerusalem
PLACES.note: 'The holy city': the devil sets Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple (4:5)

PLACES.name: Bethany beyond the Jordan
PLACES.note: Where John was baptizing (John 1:28); Jesus comes up from the water just before (3:16)

PLACES.name: Jericho
PLACES.note: A later Christian tradition places the forty days and the 'very high mountain' on the cliffs just west of Jericho (the 'Mount of Temptation'). Matthew names no place.

PLACES.name: Nazareth
PLACES.note: Jesus' hometown; next He leaves it for Capernaum (4:13)

PLACES.name: Capernaum
PLACES.note: 'By the sea, in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali' (4:13). Next episode.

PLACES.name: Gadara
PLACES.note: One of the Decapolis cities; crowds come 'from Galilee and the Decapolis' (4:25)

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 4:1-11: the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, He fasts forty days and nights, and the tempter tests Him three times. Each time Jesus answers, 'It is written,' quoting Deuteronomy. Then the devil leaves and angels minister to Him.
- Three tests, three expressions of one idea: what it means to be the Son of God. Food (appetite), rescue at the temple (affirmation from the Father), and the kingdoms of the world (power and ambition).
- The temptation is the culmination of a thread Matthew has woven since chapter 1: Jesus linked to Abraham, a Pharaoh-like Herod, a child hidden in Egypt, a baptism 'to fulfill all righteousness,' and the Father's voice, 'This is My beloved Son,' just as God called Israel His son.
- Like Israel, Jesus is led into the wilderness (the cloud and fire, Exodus 13:21), is hungry, and is tested. His answer about testing God points back to Massah, where Israel asked, 'Is Yahweh among us or not?' (Exodus 17:7).
- Behind it all is desire: Israel 'asking for food according to their desire' (Psalm 78:18) and Eve seeing that the tree was 'good for food' (Genesis 3:6). Where Adam, Eve and Israel gave in, Jesus, standing in Israel's place, says no.
- The lesson for the first hearers and for us: God's people need to be so filled and satisfied with the word of God that they stand firm in trusting Him, even in temptation. Like the Creator who rested, we learn to know when enough is enough.

## Three tests, three answers (LSB)
1. Appetite: Stones into bread
   The tempter (Matthew 4:3): "If You are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread."
   Jesus (Matthew 4:4): "It is written, ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God.’"
   It is written, Deuteronomy 8:3: "And He humbled you and let you be hungry and fed you with manna which you did not know, nor did your fathers know, that He might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by everything that proceeds out of the mouth of Yahweh." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Deuteronomy+8:3
   Israel in the wilderness: Yahweh let Israel be hungry and fed them manna, 'testing you, to know what was in your heart' (Deuteronomy 8:2-3). Later they 'put God to the test by asking for food according to their desire' (Psalm 78:18).
   The video: Satan tempts Jesus to use His 'son-of-God-ness' to eat. Jesus is truly hungry (4:2) and still trusts His Father to feed Him.
2. Affirmation: A leap from the temple
   The tempter (Matthew 4:6): "If You are the Son of God, throw Yourself down; for it is written, / ‘He will command His angels concerning You’; and / ‘On their hands they will bear You up, / Lest You strike Your foot against a stone.’"
   Jesus (Matthew 4:7): "Again, it is written, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’"
   It is written, Deuteronomy 6:16: "You shall not put Yahweh your God to the test, as you tested Him at Massah." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Deuteronomy+6:16
   Psalm in context: The devil quotes Psalm 91:11-12. The next line reads: 'You will tread upon the fierce lion and cobra, / The young lion and the serpent you will trample down' (91:13).
   Israel in the wilderness: At Massah Israel 'tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us or not?”' (Exodus 17:7). The video: with the Father not visibly present, Satan invites Jesus to force Him to show up.
   Jesus will not stage a test to prove the Father is with Him. Later He says He could appeal to His Father for 'more than twelve legions of angels' (Matthew 26:53), and still chooses the cross.
3. Ambition: All the kingdoms of the world
   The tempter (Matthew 4:9): "All these things I will give You, if You fall down and worship me."
   Jesus (Matthew 4:10): "Go, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve Him only.’"
   It is written, Deuteronomy 6:13: "Yahweh your God you shall fear; and Him you shall serve; and by His name you shall swear." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Deuteronomy+6:13
   Israel in the wilderness [Background]: The next verse warns, 'You shall not walk after other gods' (Deuteronomy 6:14). At Sinai Israel 'made for themselves a molten calf and have worshiped it' (Exodus 32:8).
   Matthew's wording ('worship... Him only') follows the Greek Old Testament tradition rather than the Hebrew 'fear.' The kingdoms Satan offers, Jesus receives later from the Father by way of the cross: 'All authority has been given to Me in heaven and on earth' (28:18).

### Back to the garden: the same desires
- Genesis 3:6 (LSB): "Then the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was desirable to make one wise, so she took from its fruit and ate; and she gave also to her husband with her, and he ate."
- (video) The teacher reads Genesis 3:6 and tracks the language of desire. Eve gave in, Israel gave in, all of us have given in; Jesus, the faithful Son, did not.
- [Debated] Some readers also line up the three tests with 'the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes and the boastful pride of life' (1 John 2:16) or with the three phrases of Genesis 3:6. The parallel is suggestive; a one-to-one match is debated. Paul draws the larger contrast: 'through the one man’s disobedience the many were appointed sinners, even so through the obedience of the One the many will be appointed righteous' (Romans 5:19).

- Then (Exodus 4:22): 'Israel is My son, My firstborn.' | Now (Matthew 3:17; 4:3): The Father: 'This is My beloved Son' (3:17). The tempter: 'If You are the Son of God' (4:3, 6).
- Then (Exodus 13:21): 'Yahweh was going before them in a pillar of cloud by day to guide them on the way.' | Now (Matthew 4:1): 'Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness.'
- Then (Deuteronomy 8:2): 'Yahweh your God has led you in the wilderness these forty years... testing you.' | Now (Matthew 4:2): 'After He had fasted forty days and forty nights, He then became hungry.' [Background]
- Then (Deuteronomy 8:3): 'He humbled you and let you be hungry and fed you with manna.' | Now (Matthew 4:3-4): Hungry, Jesus refuses to make bread for Himself and quotes this very verse.
- Then (Exodus 17:7): Israel 'tested Yahweh, saying, “Is Yahweh among us or not?”' | Now (Matthew 4:7): 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'
- Then (Psalm 78:18): 'They put God to the test / By asking for food according to their desire.' | Now (Matthew 4:1-11): Jesus denies His desires and trusts His Father.
- Then (Deuteronomy 34:1-4): From Mount Nebo, 'Yahweh showed him all the land' that Israel would receive. | Now (Matthew 4:8): The devil 'showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory.' [Background]
- Then (Exodus 32:8): Israel 'made for themselves a molten calf and have worshiped it.' | Now (Matthew 4:10): 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and serve Him only.' [Background]

## Key people
- Jesus: The beloved Son standing in the place of Israel, Yahweh's chosen servant. Where Adam, Eve and Israel gave in to desire, He refuses, answering each test with Scripture. [Background] 'One who has been tempted in all things like we are, yet without sin' (Hebrews 4:15). 'He is able to come to help those who are tempted' (Hebrews 2:18).
- The devil, the tempter, Satan: He strikes three times at one idea: what it means to be the Son of God. [Background] Matthew uses three names: 'the devil' (4:1, Greek diabolos), 'the tempter' (4:3) and 'Satan' (4:10, from Hebrew satan, 'adversary'). In the Old Testament the satan appears as an accuser in Job 1-2 and Zechariah 3. Luke adds that he left Jesus 'until an opportune time' (Luke 4:13).
- The Spirit: Leads Jesus into the wilderness, as the cloud and fire led Israel. [Background] Mark is stronger: 'the Spirit drove Him to go out into the wilderness' (Mark 1:12). Luke: Jesus was 'full of the Holy Spirit' (Luke 4:1). The same Spirit came down on Him at His baptism (3:16).
- Angels: After the devil leaves, 'angels came and began to minister to Him' (4:11). [Background] The verb (diakoneō) is also used for waiting on someone at a meal (8:15). Jesus would not force Psalm 91's angels to catch Him; afterward His Father sends them. Mark adds that 'He was with the wild beasts' (Mark 1:13).
- Israel in the wilderness: God's son, led by the cloud, tested by hunger, and failing by desire (Exodus 13, 17; Psalm 78). [Background] Deuteronomy 8:5: 'Yahweh your God was disciplining you just as a man disciplines his son.' All three of Jesus' answers come from Moses' sermons to this generation (Deuteronomy 6-8).
- Adam and Eve: The first humans, enticed by the serpent and led by desire (Genesis 3:6). [Background] Irenaeus (2nd century) reads the temptation as Jesus 're-running' Adam's test and winning it (see Early witnesses). Paul contrasts 'the one man's disobedience' with 'the obedience of the One' (Romans 5:19).
- Moses and Elijah: The video compares the child Jesus, hidden from a murderous tyrant, to Moses. It does not mention their forty-day fasts. [Background] Moses was on the mountain 'forty days and forty nights; he did not eat bread or drink water' (Exodus 34:28). Elijah went 'forty days and forty nights to Horeb' (1 Kings 19:8). Both later appear with Jesus on the mountain (17:3).

## Places [Background]
- Jerusalem: 'The holy city': the devil sets Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple (4:5)
- Bethany beyond the Jordan: Where John was baptizing (John 1:28); Jesus comes up from the water just before (3:16)
- Jericho: A later Christian tradition places the forty days and the 'very high mountain' on the cliffs just west of Jericho (the 'Mount of Temptation'). Matthew names no place.
- Nazareth: Jesus' hometown; next He leaves it for Capernaum (4:13)
- Capernaum: 'By the sea, in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali' (4:13). Next episode.
- Gadara: One of the Decapolis cities; crowds come 'from Galilee and the Decapolis' (4:25)

## Key terms
- Tempt / test: One Greek verb (peirazō) covers both. God tests to prove and strengthen (Deuteronomy 8:2); the devil tempts to make someone fall. 'God cannot be tempted by evil, and He Himself does not tempt anyone' (James 1:13). [Background]
- If You are the Son of God: The question behind all three tests. The Father has just said 'This is My beloved Son' (3:17); the tempter does not deny it but pushes Jesus to use His sonship for Himself. The same taunt returns at the cross: 'If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross' (27:40).
- It is written: Jesus' answer three times. The Greek perfect tense means 'it stands written': settled and still in force. All three quotations come from Deuteronomy 6-8.
- Forty days and forty nights: The video promises to return to numbers but does not. Forty marks testing and preparation: the flood (Genesis 7:12), Moses on the mountain (Exodus 34:28), Israel's forty years (Deuteronomy 8:2), Elijah (1 Kings 19:8). [Background]
- The holy city: Jerusalem. Matthew uses the phrase again in 27:53. [Background]
- Pinnacle of the temple: Literally 'little wing' (pterygion), some high edge of the temple complex. Matthew does not say which; many think of the southeast corner above the Kidron Valley. [Background]
- A very high mountain: Matthew names no mountain; no single peak shows 'all the kingdoms of the world.' Mountains matter in Matthew: the sermon (5:1), the transfiguration (17:1), the commission (28:16). [Background]
- Massah: 'Testing,' the place where Israel quarreled and asked, 'Is Yahweh among us or not?' (Exodus 17:7). Deuteronomy 6:16, which Jesus quotes, names it.
- Desire: The video's key word. Eve saw the tree was 'desirable' (Genesis 3:6); Israel asked for food 'according to their desire' (Psalm 78:18). 'Each one is tempted when he is carried away and enticed by his own lust' (James 1:14).

## Hebrew and Greek words [Background; Strong's numbers follow the LSB's word tagging]
- πειράζω peirazō (G3985, Greek): To test, try; to tempt. The same verb gives 'to be tempted' (4:1) and 'the tempter' (4:3, ho peirazōn, 'the one testing'). Context decides between testing and tempting. Look up: BDAG, πειράζω. (Matt 4:1, 3)
- ἐκπειράζω ekpeirazō (G1598, Greek): To put to the test. A strengthened form of peirazō, used in the Greek Old Testament of Deuteronomy 6:16 and quoted here. Look up: BDAG, ἐκπειράζω. (Matt 4:7)
- διάβολος diabolos (G1228, Greek): As an adjective 'slanderous'; as a noun 'slanderer,' and in the New Testament 'the devil.' Look up: BDAG, διάβολος. (Matt 4:1, 5, 8, 11)
- Σατανᾶς Satanas (G4567, Greek): Satan, the Greek form of Hebrew satan, 'adversary.' Jesus' 'Go' (hypage) here is the same word as 'Get behind Me, Satan!' to Peter (16:23). (Matt 4:10; 16:23)
- πτερύγιον pterygion (G4419, Greek): Diminutive of pteryx, 'wing': a tip or edge, here a high point of the temple. Which spot is meant is uncertain. Look up: BDAG, πτερύγιον. (Matt 4:5)
- προσκυνέω proskyneō (G4352, Greek): To bow down, prostrate oneself; to worship. The magi came to 'worship' Jesus (2:2, 11); Satan asks Jesus to 'fall down and worship' him. (Matt 4:9, 10; 2:2, 11)
- λατρεύω latreuō (G3000, Greek): To serve, especially in worship. Translates Hebrew 'abad' (serve) in Deuteronomy 6:13. (Matt 4:10)
- διακονέω diakoneō (G1247, Greek): To serve, wait on, minister; used of serving at a meal. The angels 'began to minister' after His long hunger (4:11; compare 8:15). (Matt 4:11; 8:15)
- ῥῆμα rhēma (G4487, Greek): Word, saying, something spoken. 'Every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God' (4:4), the verse behind the channel's name. (Matt 4:4)
- נָסָה nasah (H5254, Hebrew): To test, try, prove. Used for God testing Israel (Deuteronomy 8:2) and Israel testing God (Exodus 17:7; Deuteronomy 6:16). Look up: BDB or HALOT, נסה. (Deut 6:16; 8:2; Exod 17:7)
- מַסָּה massah (H4532, Hebrew): 'Testing,' a place name from nasah. Exodus 17:7 explains the name: 'because they tested Yahweh.' (Exod 17:7; Deut 6:16)
- מוֹצָא motsa (H4161, Hebrew): That which goes out, an utterance. 'Everything that proceeds out of the mouth of Yahweh' (Deuteronomy 8:3). Look up: BDB or HALOT, מוֹצָא. (Deut 8:3)
- עָבַד abad (H5647, Hebrew): To work, serve; also to serve in worship. 'Him you shall serve' (Deuteronomy 6:13). (Deut 6:13)
- שָׂטָן satan (H7854, Hebrew): Adversary, accuser; with the article, 'the satan' (Job 1:6; Zechariah 3:1). Look up: BDB or HALOT, שָׂטָן. (Job 1:6; Zech 3:1)

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- All three answers: Deuteronomy 6-8: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell preaching to Israel on the plains of Moab, after forty years in the wilderness. Jesus quotes 8:3, 6:16 and 6:13, close to the Shema: 'Hear, O Israel! Yahweh is our God, Yahweh is one! You shall love Yahweh your God with all your heart' (6:4-5). Matthew's wording follows the Greek Old Testament: 'every word' (8:3) and 'worship... Him only' (6:13).
- Three Gospels, one test: Mark gives two verses (1:12-13). Matthew and Luke give the three tests, but Luke has the temple last (Luke 4:5-12), while Matthew ends on the mountain, with worship. Matthew links the scene to the baptism: 'Then' (4:1).
- The temple Satan stood Him on: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple and its courts in his eighteenth year, about 20/19 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 15.11.1). Josephus describes the royal portico on the south side as so high above the valley that anyone looking down would grow dizzy (Antiquities 15.11.5).
- Fasting forty days: Moses (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 9:9) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:8) both went forty days without ordinary food. Matthew says Jesus 'fasted' (4:2); Luke says 'He ate nothing during those days' (Luke 4:2). Only afterward did He become hungry.
- Psalm 91 in context: A psalm of trust: whoever shelters in the Most High is guarded by His angels. The devil quotes 91:11-12 as a dare. The psalm's promise is for those who trust God, not for those who test Him.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- Irenaeus of Lyons (c. AD 180): "For as at the beginning it was by means of food that [the enemy] persuaded man, although not suffering hunger, to transgress God's commandments, so in the end he did not succeed in persuading Him that was an hungered to take that food which proceeded from God." Against Heresies 5.21.2, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (public domain). Of the second test he writes that the devil was 'concealing a falsehood under the guise of Scripture.'
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Then. When? After the descent of the Spirit, after the voice that was borne from above, and said, This is My Beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Homilies on Matthew 13, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain). He also says Jesus answered 'bringing him a testimony out of the ancient Scripture.'

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Matthew's order or Luke's? Luke has the temple last; Matthew has the mountain last. Many think Matthew's order builds to the climax of worship ('Go, Satan!'), while Luke's ends at Jerusalem, the goal of his Gospel. Neither writer says his order is chronological.
- Physical journey or vision? No mountain shows 'all the kingdoms of the world,' so some read the second and third tests as visionary. Others take the journeys as real, with the 'showing' supernatural. Matthew says the devil 'took Him' (4:5, 8) and does not explain how.
- Could Jesus have sinned? Hebrews says He was tempted 'in all things like we are, yet without sin' (4:15). Theologians differ on whether He was able not to sin or not able to sin; all agree the testing was real. The video puts it simply: 'Jesus is the God-man, and there are things only He could go through.'
- Do the three tests match Genesis 3:6 or 1 John 2:16? Some line up food, eyes and pride one for one; others think that is too neat. The video links them more loosely, through the language of desire.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says Herod 'killed firstborns.' Matthew 2:16 says he killed 'all the male children who were in Bethlehem and all its vicinity, from two years old and under.' Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew son killed (Exodus 1:22); the death of the firstborn was the tenth plague, on Egypt (Exodus 12:29). The Pharaoh parallel still holds.
- The video promises, 'We're going to get into numbers and what they mean later,' but does not come back to the forty days. See Key terms and the Timeline for a start.
- The video calls Matthew 'probably a letter that's being read to the church.' Matthew is a Gospel, not a letter, though the teacher's point stands: it was likely heard read aloud by early believers.
- Among the Isaiah references, the video lists 'the true vine' (John 15:1). The words are Jesus' own in John; the Old Testament picture behind them is Israel as God's vine (Psalm 80:8; Isaiah 5:1-7).
- The captions read 'Matthew 4:1-1'; the passage is Matthew 4:1-11.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. The video's own challenge: 'If God's people need to be so filled and satisfied with the word of God that they can stand firm in trusting Him even in the midst of temptation, then will you?' What would that look like for you this week?
2. All three of Jesus' answers come from Deuteronomy 6-8. Read those three chapters. What else there would have strengthened Him, and you?
3. Appetite, affirmation, ambition: which of the three hits closest to home? Where do you need to tell a desire, 'No, I will not be ruled by you'?
4. The devil quoted Scripture too (Psalm 91). How can you tell Scripture used rightly from Scripture twisted? Read Psalm 91 whole and compare.

## Application
- (video) The video's lesson for the original audience: to withstand the devil, who entices God's people to give in to their own desires, we must be filled with the word of God and so satisfied with it that we stand firm in trusting the Lord, His provision and His plans. Where mankind failed, Jesus succeeded. Like our Creator, who stopped and saw that His work was good, we learn to know when enough is enough. The lesson for you: will you be filled and satisfied with the word of God?
- Study note (added): Jesus did not invent new weapons; He used verses Israel had known for centuries, in context. Treasure the word now, before the test comes: 'Your word I have treasured in my heart, / That I may not sin against You' (Psalm 119:11). 'The sword of the Spirit... is the word of God' (Ephesians 6:17). And when you fail, the One who passed the test is 'able to come to help those who are tempted' (Hebrews 2:18; see 1 Corinthians 10:13).
